inputs.trustName: The Alex Morgan Special Needs Trust

expectedText:
SPECIAL NEEDS TRUST
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Morgan

DECLARATION
I, Pat Morgan, as settlor, declare that I am creating the The Alex Morgan Special Needs Trust for the benefit of Alex Morgan, and that I am transferring the property described in the attached schedule to Jordan Morgan, as initial trustee, to hold, administer, and distribute according to the terms of this trust. This trust is intended to qualify as a special needs trust — a trust structured so that its assets are not treated as available to Alex Morgan for purposes of eligibility for means-tested government benefits. Upon the death, resignation, or incapacity of Jordan Morgan, Casey Morgan shall serve as successor trustee.

FIRST-PARTY (SELF-SETTLED) SPECIAL NEEDS TRUSTS — FEDERAL STATUTORY BASIS
Federal Medicaid law creates a specific, narrow exception for a trust that holds a disabled individual's own assets: such a trust is excluded from Medicaid's general trust-counting rules if it meets each of several conditions set by statute — the individual is under age 65, the individual meets the federal definition of disability used elsewhere in the Social Security Act, and the trust is established for that individual's benefit by the individual, a parent, grandparent, legal guardian, or a court. This is federal law that applies the same way regardless of which state administers the Medicaid program — in California, Medi-Cal — and every other state's Medicaid program applies this same federal floor, though a state may add its own procedural requirements on top of it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A trust containing the assets of an individual under age 65 who is disabled (as defined in section 1382c(a)(3) of this title) and which is established for the benefit of such individual by the individual, a parent, grandparent, legal guardian of the individual, or a court if the State will receive all amounts remaining in the trust upon the death of such individual up to an amount equal to the total medical assistance paid on behalf of the individual under a State plan under this subchapter."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4)(A), the federal Medicaid statute's exception for a first-party special needs trust (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1396p)
  Known gap: This exception is codified at a specific, narrow point in the Medicaid statute — it does not create a general "special needs trust" category, only this one described combination of facts. A trust that departs from these conditions (for example, one established by someone other than the parties this statute lists, or established after the individual turns 65) does not automatically qualify, regardless of how it labels itself. Medicaid separately defines "disabled" for this purpose by cross-reference to the same definition used for Supplemental Security Income eligibility (a functional test tied to a medically determinable impairment and inability to engage in substantial gainful activity). A related paragraph of this same statute creates a separate, additionally-conditioned exception for pooled trusts managed by a non-profit association — a related but distinct arrangement not covered in this clause. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1396p(d)(4)(A)); no additional independent source was found for this.

THE MEDICAID PAYBACK REQUIREMENT
The same statutory exception that allows a first-party special needs trust to hold a disabled individual's own assets without those assets counting against Medicaid eligibility comes with a mandatory condition attached to the same sentence: the state must be repaid, out of whatever remains in the trust when the individual dies, up to the total amount of Medicaid benefits paid on that individual's behalf during their life. This payback obligation runs to the state that administered the Medicaid benefits — in California, the state Department of Health Care Services, which administers Medi-Cal — and applies regardless of who else the trust names as a remainder beneficiary; whatever the trust document says about where the remaining property should go after death, this statutory payback claim applies first, up to the amount owed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A trust containing the assets of an individual under age 65 who is disabled (as defined in section 1382c(a)(3) of this title) and which is established for the benefit of such individual by the individual, a parent, grandparent, legal guardian of the individual, or a court if the State will receive all amounts remaining in the trust upon the death of such individual up to an amount equal to the total medical assistance paid on behalf of the individual under a State plan under this subchapter."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4)(A) [payback], the state Medicaid payback requirement attached to the first-party trust exception (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1396p)
  Known gap: This condition is not a separate statute — it is part of the same sentence, same statutory subsection, 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(4)(A), as the eligibility conditions in the preceding clause; it is presented separately here because it is one of the most consequential and most often misunderstood features of a first-party special needs trust, not because it comes from an independent source. The statute does not describe a payback capped at some lesser amount — it states the state receives amounts remaining in the trust up to the total medical assistance paid, meaning the payback claim can absorb the entire remainder if that remainder doesn't exceed what Medicaid paid. How this federal payback claim is actually processed, and what (if anything) is deducted before it is satisfied, is governed by the administering state's own Medicaid program rather than by this federal provision itself. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1396p(d)(4)(A)); no additional independent source was found for this.

THIRD-PARTY SPECIAL NEEDS TRUSTS — NO STATUTORY PAYBACK (A STRUCTURAL, NOT A STANDALONE, EXCEPTION)
A trust funded with someone else's own money — for example, a parent's or grandparent's own assets, never owned by the disabled beneficiary — is treated differently under federal Medicaid law than the first-party trust described above. The same subsection that creates Medicaid's trust-counting rules applies, by its own terms, only to a trust the statute treats as "established by" the individual, and the statute defines that phrase to require that the individual's own assets were used to form the trust's corpus. A trust funded exclusively with a third party's own assets, and established by that third party, does not meet the statute's definition of a trust "established by" the individual in the first place — so the trust-counting subsection, including its payback condition, never applies to it at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(1) For purposes of determining an individual's eligibility for, or amount of, benefits under a State plan under this subchapter, subject to paragraph (4), the rules specified in paragraph (3) shall apply to a trust established by such individual. (2)(A) For purposes of this subsection, an individual shall be considered to have established a trust if assets of the individual were used to form all or part of the corpus of the trust and if any of the following individuals established such trust other than by will: (i) The individual. (ii) The individual's spouse. (iii) A person, including a court or administrative body, with legal authority to act in place of or on behalf of the individual or the individual's spouse. (iv) A person, including any court or administrative body, acting at the direction or upon the request of the individual or the individual's spouse."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d)(1), (d)(2)(A), the definition of a trust 'established by' an individual, and the scope of Medicaid's trust-counting rules (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1396p)
  Known gap: This is a real and important distinction, but it is honestly a structural consequence of how the statute defines "established by the individual," not a separate, standalone statutory exception written the way the first-party trust exception is — there is no subsection stating, in so many words, that a third-party special needs trust is exempt from payback. If the trust in fact contains any of the beneficiary's own assets — for instance, because the beneficiary contributed some of their own funds — the trust-counting rules can attach to that portion regardless of what the trust calls itself. This clause draws on the same statutory section as the two preceding clauses — 42 U.S.C. § 1396p(d) — but a different paragraph of it (the definitional paragraphs (d)(1) and (d)(2)(A), rather than the specific-exception paragraph (d)(4)(A)); it is not an independently sourced statutory rule. Whether a particular trust actually qualifies as a pure third-party trust under this reasoning is a fact-specific determination the statute does not spell out in a single clean rule. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 1396p(d)); no additional independent source was found for this.

SSI'S RESOURCE LIMIT AND WHEN TRUST ASSETS ARE NOT A COUNTABLE RESOURCE
Supplemental Security Income eligibility is subject to a strict cap on countable resources set by Social Security Administration regulation: $2,000 for an individual, and $3,000 for an individual with an eligible spouse — a figure the regulation has held constant since it took effect January 1, 1989. Separately, SSA's general resource-counting regulation defines a "resource" as property the individual owns and could convert to cash for support and maintenance, and it ties that specifically to whether the individual has the legal right, authority, or power to liquidate the property: property a person cannot liquidate is not counted as their resource at all. A properly structured special needs trust is built around that second rule — its terms are meant to ensure the beneficiary has no legal right to demand principal or compel distributions, so trust assets are not something the beneficiary "could convert to cash," rather than around any special trust-specific exclusion written into the resource-limit regulation itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(c) Effective January 1, 1985 and later. The resources limits and effective dates for January 1, 1985 and later are as follows: Effective date Individual Individual and spouse Jan. 1, 1985 $1,600 $2,400 Jan. 1, 1986 1,700 $2,550 Jan. 1, 1987 1,800 $2,700 Jan. 1, 1988 1,900 $2,850 Jan. 1, 1989 2,000 $3,000"
  — 20 C.F.R. § 416.1205(c), the SSI individual and couple resource limits (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/416.1205)
  "If the individual has the right, authority or power to liquidate the property or his or her share of the property, it is considered a resource. If a property right cannot be liquidated, the property will not be considered a resource of the individual (or spouse)."
  — 20 C.F.R. § 416.1201(a)(1), the general availability / right-to-liquidate test for what counts as a resource (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/20/416.1201)
  Known gap: These are two distinct SSA regulations within the same regulatory part (20 C.F.R. Part 416, Subpart L) — the dollar limit (§ 416.1205) and the general availability test (§ 416.1201) — genuinely different sections addressing different questions, not subsections of one provision. Neither regulation specifically defines when trust assets are or are not "available"; SSA's more detailed, trust-specific counting rules for SSI purposes live in a different statutory provision (42 U.S.C. § 1382b(e)) and in the agency's own sub-regulatory guidance (its Program Operations Manual System), which were not independently fetched or verified here and are not cited as authority in this clause. On the dollar figure itself: the source regulation's own citation shows it was last amended in 1985 (50 FR 38982) and its table has not been updated since the $2,000/$3,000 figures took effect in 1989 — this source shows no later change to that number. Whether any particular trust's own terms in fact deny the beneficiary the kind of access this rule turns on — commonly built around "sole benefit of the beneficiary" and fully discretionary, no-demand-right distribution language — is a drafting and administration question the regulation itself does not resolve.

DISCRETIONARY DISTRIBUTION STANDARD — SOLE BENEFIT
The trustee shall use the trust property solely for the benefit of Alex Morgan and for no other person's benefit, applying distributions to supplement — and not replace — any benefits Alex Morgan receives or may become eligible to receive from any government program. All distributions of income or principal are within the trustee's sole and absolute discretion; Alex Morgan has no right to demand or compel any distribution, and no power to assign, direct, or anticipate any interest in the trust property. ☐ The trustee's discretion is limited as follows: None

ABLE ACCOUNTS — A DISTINCT, SIMPLER FEDERAL SAVINGS VEHICLE (NOT A TRUST)
Separate from any trust, federal tax law authorizes a different kind of vehicle for a person with a disability to save money without losing means-tested benefits: a "qualified ABLE program" account, created by the ABLE Act of 2014 and codified in the Internal Revenue Code. An ABLE account is a state-administered savings account, not a trust — one account per eligible beneficiary, funded with cash contributions, invested and managed by the state program rather than by an individually chosen trustee. Eligibility is limited to a person whose blindness or disability began before a statutory age cutoff — currently age 46 — established either through existing Social Security disability/blindness benefits or a separate disability-certification process. A companion federal provision directs that ABLE account funds are disregarded for most means-tested federal programs, and specifically for SSI, up to $100,000 in an ABLE account is disregarded as a resource; amounts above $100,000 do count as an SSI resource (suspending, rather than terminating, SSI eligibility), while Medicaid eligibility is unaffected by the account's balance regardless of amount.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A program shall not be treated as a qualified ABLE program unless it provides that no contribution will be accepted— (A) unless it is in cash, or (B) except in the case of contributions under subsection (c)(1)(C) or received in a qualified ABLE rollover contribution described in section 530A(d)(4)(B), if such contribution to an ABLE account would result in aggregate contributions from all contributors to the ABLE account for the taxable year exceeding the sum of— (i) the amount in effect under section 2503(b) (determined by substituting "1996" for "1997" in paragraph (2)(B) thereof) for the calendar year in which the taxable year begins, plus (ii) in the case of any contribution by a designated beneficiary described in paragraph (7), the lesser of— (I) compensation (as defined by section 219(f)(1)) includible in the designated beneficiary's gross income for the taxable year, or (II) an amount equal to the poverty line for a one-person household, as determined for the calendar year preceding the calendar year in which the taxable year begins."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 529A(b)(2), the qualified ABLE program contribution cap, cross-referenced to the annual gift-tax exclusion (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/529A)
  "An individual is an eligible individual for a taxable year if during such taxable year— (A) the individual is entitled to benefits based on blindness or disability under title II or XVI of the Social Security Act, and such blindness or disability occurred before the date on which the individual attained age 46, or (B) a disability certification with respect to such individual is filed with the Secretary for such taxable year."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 529A(e)(1), the age-of-onset eligibility requirement for a designated beneficiary (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/529A)
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of Federal law that requires consideration of 1 or more financial circumstances of an individual, for the purpose of determining eligibility to receive, or the amount of, any assistance or benefit authorized by such provision to be provided to or for the benefit of such individual, any amount (including earnings thereon) in the ABLE account (within the meaning of section 529A of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986) of such individual, any contributions to the ABLE account of the individual, and any distribution for qualified disability expenses (as defined in subsection (e)(5) of such section) shall be disregarded for such purpose with respect to any period during which such individual maintains, makes contributions to, or receives distributions from such ABLE account, except that, in the case of the supplemental security income program under title XVI of the Social Security Act [42 U.S.C. 1381 et seq.]— (1) a distribution for housing expenses (within the meaning of such subsection) shall not be so disregarded, and (2) in the case of such program, any amount (including such earnings) in such ABLE account shall be considered a resource of the designated beneficiary to the extent that such amount exceeds $100,000."
  — Pub. L. 113-295, div. B, title I, § 103(a), the federal means-tested-program disregard for ABLE account funds, including the $100,000 SSI resource threshold (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/529A)
  Known gap: Annual contributions to an ABLE account are capped, but the statute sets that cap by cross-reference to the federal annual gift-tax exclusion amount under 26 U.S.C. § 2503(b) — a figure the IRS adjusts for inflation most years — rather than stating a fixed dollar number in the ABLE statute itself; that current inflation-adjusted figure was not independently verified from a primary source here and is not stated as a specific number in this clause. The contribution-structure and eligibility-age citations below are both drawn from the same Internal Revenue Code section, 26 U.S.C. § 529A, just different subsections; the SSI/Medicaid-treatment citation is a genuinely separate source — an uncodified note under Pub. L. 113-295 rather than the operative Code section itself. An ABLE account is materially smaller in what it can hold and simpler to set up than a special needs trust, but it is not a substitute for one in every case — among other differences, it carries its own $100,000 SSI-resource-disregard ceiling and its own age-of-onset eligibility requirement, neither of which applies to a special needs trust.

CALIFORNIA'S SPECIAL NEEDS TRUST STATUTE — NARROWER THAN IT SOUNDS
California's Probate Code does use the specific term "special needs trust," but only within a narrow chapter governing court-approved compromises, settlements, and judgments for a minor or a person with a disability — not as a general estate-planning statute for special needs trusts created outside that litigation context. The chapter applies only when a court approves a compromise or covenant not to sue on a minor's disputed claim, approves a compromise of a pending action involving a minor or person with a disability, or enters judgment for one of them, and the resulting money or property is to be paid or delivered for that person's benefit. Within that chapter, a separate section authorizes the court to order that such money be paid into a special needs trust instead of directly to the minor or person with a disability, requires the court to make specific findings before doing so, and keeps the resulting trust under the court's continuing jurisdiction.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "This chapter applies whenever both of the following conditions exist: (a) A court (1) approves a compromise of, or the execution of a covenant not to sue on or a covenant not to enforce judgment on, a minor's disputed claim, (2) approves a compromise of a pending action or proceeding to which a minor or person with a disability is a party, or (3) gives judgment for a minor or person with a disability. (b) The compromise, covenant, or judgment provides for the payment or delivery of money or other property for the benefit of the minor or person with a disability."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 3600, the scope of Probate Code Chapter 4's protective proceedings for a minor's or disabled person's litigation recovery (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=3600.)
  "(a)(1) If a court makes an order under Section 3602 or 3611 that money of a minor or person with a disability be paid to a special needs trust, the terms of the trust shall be reviewed and approved by the court and shall satisfy the requirements of this section. The trust is subject to continuing jurisdiction of the court, and is subject to court supervision to the extent determined by the court. The court may transfer jurisdiction to the court in the proper county for commencement of a proceeding as determined under Section 17005."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 3604(a)(1), the court-ordered special needs trust mechanism itself (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=3604.)
  "(b) A special needs trust may be established and continued under this section only if the court determines all of the following: (1) That the minor or person with a disability has a disability that substantially impairs the individual's ability to provide for the individual's own care or custody and constitutes a substantial handicap. (2) That the minor or person with a disability is likely to have special needs that will not be met without the trust. (3) That money to be paid to the trust does not exceed the amount that appears reasonably necessary to meet the special needs of the minor or person with a disability."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 3604(b), the findings the court must make before establishing the trust (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=3604.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, not a description of special needs trusts generally — its "special needs trust" only exists as a mechanism for money a court is itself directing out of a settlement, covenant, or judgment; it is not a vehicle a family can independently establish outside a lawsuit under this particular statute. A trust created outside this litigation context — for example, funded with a parent's own estate-planning assets rather than a court-approved settlement — is not governed by this chapter, and instead depends on general trust law and the federal Medicaid/SSI rules addressed elsewhere in this document, not on Cal. Prob. Code §§ 3600-3613. The two citations below (§ 3604(a)(1) and § 3604(b)) are subsections of the same code section, presented separately here only for readability, not as independent sources from each other; § 3600 is a genuinely different section.

SIGNATURE AND NOTARIZATION
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, Pat Morgan, as settlor, and Jordan Morgan, as trustee, have signed this trust instrument on the date written below.

☐ _________________________ Date: _______________
Pat Morgan, Settlor

☐ _________________________ Date: _______________
Jordan Morgan, Trustee

A notary public or other officer completing a notarial certificate for this instrument verifies only the identity of the individual who signed the document, not the truthfulness, accuracy, or validity of that document.

A companion federal provision directs that ABLE account funds are disregarded for most means-tested federal programs, and specifically for SSI, up to $100,000 in an ABLE account is disregarded as a resource; amounts above $100,000 do count as an SSI resource (suspending, rather than terminating, SSI eligibility), while Medicaid eligibility is unaffected by the account's balance regardless of amount.

citations.cite: the qualified ABLE program contribution cap, cross-referenced to the annual gift-tax exclusion
citations.quote: A program shall not be treated as a qualified ABLE program unless it provides that no contribution will be accepted— (A) unless it is in cash, or (B) except in the case of contributions under subsection (c)(1)(C) or received in a qualified ABLE rollover contribution described in section 530A(d)(4)(B), if such contribution to an ABLE account would result in aggregate contributions from all contributors to the ABLE account for the taxable year exceeding the sum of— (i) the amount in effect under section 2503(b) (determined by substituting "1996" for "1997" in paragraph (2)(B) thereof) for the calendar year in which the taxable year begins, plus (ii) in the case of any contribution by a designated beneficiary described in paragraph (7), the lesser of— (I) compensation (as defined by section 219(f)(1)) includible in the designated beneficiary's gross income for the taxable year, or (II) an amount equal to the poverty line for a one-person household, as determined for the calendar year preceding the calendar year in which the taxable year begins.

citations.cite: the age-of-onset eligibility requirement for a designated beneficiary
citations.quote: An individual is an eligible individual for a taxable year if during such taxable year— (A) the individual is entitled to benefits based on blindness or disability under title II or XVI of the Social Security Act, and such blindness or disability occurred before the date on which the individual attained age 46, or (B) a disability certification with respect to such individual is filed with the Secretary for such taxable year.

citations.case: Pub. L. 113-295, div. B, title I, § 103(a)
citations.cite: the federal means-tested-program disregard for ABLE account funds, including the $100,000 SSI resource threshold
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of Federal law that requires consideration of 1 or more financial circumstances of an individual, for the purpose of determining eligibility to receive, or the amount of, any assistance or benefit authorized by such provision to be provided to or for the benefit of such individual, any amount (including earnings thereon) in the ABLE account (within the meaning of section 529A of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986) of such individual, any contributions to the ABLE account of the individual, and any distribution for qualified disability expenses (as defined in subsection (e)(5) of such section) shall be disregarded for such purpose with respect to any period during which such individual maintains, makes contributions to, or receives distributions from such ABLE account, except that, in the case of the supplemental security income program under title XVI of the Social Security Act [42 U.S.C. 1381 et seq.]— (1) a distribution for housing expenses (within the meaning of such subsection) shall not be so disregarded, and (2) in the case of such program, any amount (including such earnings) in such ABLE account shall be considered a resource of the designated beneficiary to the extent that such amount exceeds $100,000.

expectedJSON.gap: Annual contributions to an ABLE account are capped, but the statute sets that cap by cross-reference to the federal annual gift-tax exclusion amount under 26 U.S.C. § 2503(b) — a figure the IRS adjusts for inflation most years — rather than stating a fixed dollar number in the ABLE statute itself; that current inflation-adjusted figure was not independently verified from a primary source here and is not stated as a specific number in this clause. The contribution-structure and eligibility-age citations below are both drawn from the same Internal Revenue Code section, 26 U.S.C. § 529A, just different subsections; the SSI/Medicaid-treatment citation is a genuinely separate source — an uncodified note under Pub. L. 113-295 rather than the operative Code section itself. An ABLE account is materially smaller in what it can hold and simpler to set up than a special needs trust, but it is not a substitute for one in every case — among other differences, it carries its own $100,000 SSI-resource-disregard ceiling and its own age-of-onset eligibility requirement, neither of which applies to a special needs trust.

expectedJSON.body: California's Probate Code does use the specific term "special needs trust," but only within a narrow chapter governing court-approved compromises, settlements, and judgments for a minor or a person with a disability — not as a general estate-planning statute for special needs trusts created outside that litigation context. The chapter applies only when a court approves a compromise or covenant not to sue on a minor's disputed claim, approves a compromise of a pending action involving a minor or person with a disability, or enters judgment for one of them, and the resulting money or property is to be paid or delivered for that person's benefit. Within that chapter, a separate section authorizes the court to order that such money be paid into a special needs trust instead of directly to the minor or person with a disability, requires the court to make specific findings before doing so, and keeps the resulting trust under the court's continuing jurisdiction.

citations.cite: the scope of Probate Code Chapter 4's protective proceedings for a minor's or disabled person's litigation recovery
citations.quote: This chapter applies whenever both of the following conditions exist: (a) A court (1) approves a compromise of, or the execution of a covenant not to sue on or a covenant not to enforce judgment on, a minor's disputed claim, (2) approves a compromise of a pending action or proceeding to which a minor or person with a disability is a party, or (3) gives judgment for a minor or person with a disability. (b) The compromise, covenant, or judgment provides for the payment or delivery of money or other property for the benefit of the minor or person with a disability.

citations.cite: the court-ordered special needs trust mechanism itself
citations.quote: (a)(1) If a court makes an order under Section 3602 or 3611 that money of a minor or person with a disability be paid to a special needs trust, the terms of the trust shall be reviewed and approved by the court and shall satisfy the requirements of this section. The trust is subject to continuing jurisdiction of the court, and is subject to court supervision to the extent determined by the court. The court may transfer jurisdiction to the court in the proper county for commencement of a proceeding as determined under Section 17005.

citations.cite: the findings the court must make before establishing the trust
citations.quote: (b) A special needs trust may be established and continued under this section only if the court determines all of the following: (1) That the minor or person with a disability has a disability that substantially impairs the individual's ability to provide for the individual's own care or custody and constitutes a substantial handicap. (2) That the minor or person with a disability is likely to have special needs that will not be met without the trust. (3) That money to be paid to the trust does not exceed the amount that appears reasonably necessary to meet the special needs of the minor or person with a disability.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute, not a description of special needs trusts generally — its "special needs trust" only exists as a mechanism for money a court is itself directing out of a settlement, covenant, or judgment; it is not a vehicle a family can independently establish outside a lawsuit under this particular statute. A trust created outside this litigation context — for example, funded with a parent's own estate-planning assets rather than a court-approved settlement — is not governed by this chapter, and instead depends on general trust law and the federal Medicaid/SSI rules addressed elsewhere in this document, not on Cal. Prob. Code §§ 3600-3613. The two citations below (§ 3604(a)(1) and § 3604(b)) are subsections of the same code section, presented separately here only for readability, not as independent sources from each other; § 3600 is a genuinely different section.
